data.title: Alarm and Monitoring Response Untested
data.summary: Intrusion detection was installed but its response was never exercised: activations produced no attendance within a useful time, and in places no activation reached anyone at all.
data.description:
An alarm is a notification, not a control. What protects the site is the response: somebody attending, promptly, and knowing what to do.

The failures are in the chain rather than the sensors. Activations route to a console nobody watches out of hours; the monitoring contract specifies an attendance time nobody has measured; a history of false alarms has trained staff to clear activations without investigating; and zones have been disabled to stop nuisance alerts, with no record of which.

Testing the alarm — the usual practice — confirms the sensor and the siren. It does not confirm that a person arrives, which is the part an intruder is betting against.
data.recommendation:
* Test the response rather than the alarm: trigger a zone unannounced and measure what happens and how long it takes.
* Review which zones are disabled or in fault, and treat a disabled zone as an open door.
* Investigate repeated false activations as a reliability problem, since they train the response away.
* Confirm the out-of-hours path reaches a person with the authority to act, and rehearse it.
data.short_recommendation: Test the response, not the alarm, and measure how long it takes.
